7	I was born in nineteen twelve at the top end of Ostrey Hollow, in the house my father's father put up, and except for two years down at Ashlin when I was first married I have never lived anywhere else, and I would not count those two years anyhow. My father hauled milk to the station the same as everybody up here did. There were nine families of us hauling to that station and we were in and out of each other's kitchens the whole year round and I could name you every one of them, but you don't want names, you want the trouble, they always want the trouble.
8	
9	The station stood at the very top of the Hollow where the road bends and then goes to nothing but the ridge. It was a low building, whitewashed, cold as a spring house inside even in August, and it smelled of milk and steam and hot iron, and you could hear the engine going before you came round the last turn. Ansel Keddie ran it. He went up there in ninety-five, the year before they opened it, to get it ready, and he tested that first summer too, and he was still there when I was a girl big enough to ride on the wagon with my father, so you can count that up and see how long a man can stand in one room.
10	
11	He kept a book. I want to say about that book because everybody knew about it, it wasn't any secret thing. It was ruled, and the ruling was his own, done with a straightedge, and every line in it was the same height as every other line, and his figures were like print. He wrote in it standing up at a slope desk by the window where the light came in. If a man came in and asked him what his milk had done, he did not have to hunt. He turned to the day and he read it off. He tested a thousand cans a week and never a blot in that book, and I heard my father say more than once that if the rest of the world kept its accounts the way Ansel Keddie kept his there would be no lawyers in Ashlin. Which was my father's way of talking. There are still lawyers in Ashlin.

13	Now. Nineteen nineteen. That is the year everything went sour up here and I was seven years old and I remember it the way you remember a smell. A letter came from the Association, printed, over the manager's signature, and it said there was water in the cans coming down from Ostrey Hollow. That is what it said. Water in the cans. It went to nine families and my father was one of the nine and he read it at the table with his hat still on, which he never did, and my mother stood at the stove with her back to him and did not turn around the whole time he read it. He read it twice. Then he put it in the drawer of the desk in the front room and it was still in that drawer when he died and I believe my brother has it yet. Some of them kept theirs till they died. One woman I knew had hers pinned inside the lid of her trunk. You can tell people a thing like that is only business and they will still keep the paper forty years to prove what was said of them.

472	Since you asked me particularly about water, I will answer it flatly. A cheesemaker knows watered milk inside a day. He does not need a test to know it, though the test will tell him too. The curd comes soft and it will not knit; you get a slack, weak body and your yield is down, and you can stand at the vat and see your money going out with the whey. It cannot be hidden from the man who makes the cheese, because the cheese tells him, and it tells him the next morning, not next year. Butter is more forgiving that way. Cheese is a witness. In sixteen summers my father never made one complaint of those four men, never docked one of them a cent, and never — not once that I heard, and I was in the room — said a word about their milk except that he wished he had more of it in July.

505	
506	This station has been asked, at intervals for fifty years, why the butterfat tests at one skimming station in Ordell County ran below those of its own creamery seven miles down the same valley. ## Section A — Reconstruction

### Story 1 — The Association and the Rule That Made the Test the Master (1889–1892; the office to 1945)

**Who.** The farmers of the Larrow Valley, Ordell County; Gideon Vose, first president; the office that later administered his rule — Effie Loomis (secretary 1901–1940), Wilbur Teague (bookkeeper 1905–1945), Hobart Sill (buttermaker at Larrow Green 1893–1934), Bertram Kyle (outer-desk clerk), and Selby Vose, Gideon's **son** [not nephew, as Toland and Rundle have it — Selby's own printed words: "My father, who was your first president"], manager 1913–1938 [Kyle's 1911 is wrong].

**What happened.** In 1889 the valley's farmers met at Larrow Green (the schoolhouse, by valley memory) and organized the Larrow Valley Cooperative Creamery Association, tired of taking the Ashlin merchant's price for butter. Gideon Vose was elected president and held it twenty-two years, to 1911; he died in 1917. Not a lawyer, he wrote the by-laws himself at his kitchen table. In 1891 the main creamery was built at Larrow Green on Larrow Creek and the valley began to be paid in cash monthly. Before it, every man's arithmetic was his own.

The by-law that governs everything afterward is **Article VII**: every patron is paid according to the pounds of butterfat in his milk "ascertained by test, and not according to the weight of the milk; and the test of the station where he delivers shall govern." The last clause is the hinge. It allows no appeal to the creamery's test, the valley average, or any retest: the instrument at a man's own station is the whole]

## Section A — Reconstruction (continued)

### Story 5 — "Station Gain, Five and a Quarter Per Cent, As Usual" (1897–1925)

**Who.** Wilbur Teague, bookkeeper 1905–1945; Hobart Sill, buttermaker, keeper of the receiving and churn books; Bertram Kyle, the clerk who copied the line every year; Selby Vose, who signed the annual sheet.

**What happened.** Because the station separated on the spot and the cream came down to Larrow Green, the Association held two figures for the same fat: what the station's tests credited to the patrons, and what was weighed and tested into the vats at Larrow Green. The second was always larger. The 1898 entry, complete: "Ostrey Hollow: butter fat credited to patrons on station test, 57,760 lb. Butter fat received at Larrow Green in station cream, 60,800 lb. Station gain, 3,040 lb, five and a quarter per cent, as usual. Carried to the general account." The line stands in that form for every year of the station column, which begins 1897 [Teague's claim to have invented it in 1905 is contradicted by the 1898 entry he himself quotes]. Sill weighed the Hollow cream over again himself and wrote it in the receiving book from 1893: it "ran heavy. Every year… Always more. Never less" — and he made nothing of it, and nobody asked. Kyle copied the line "more times than I can count" and never wondered: a figure with a name on it has been explained.

The percentages: 3,040 is 5¼ % of the 57,760 **credited** and 5 % of the 60,800 **received** — Teague and Vaught both say "of the fat actually delivered," the wrong denominator. ## Section C — Math

### C1

**(a) Proportion.** Nine surviving pipettes, stems blown 17.6 c.c., delivered against a calibrated burette (mean of five runs each): 16.70, 16.71, 16.72, 16.72, 16.72, 16.73, 16.73, 16.74, 16.71. Sum = 150.48; ÷ 9 = **16.72 c.c.** Ratio 16.72 ÷ 17.6 = **0.95 exactly** (17.6 × 0.95 = 16.72). The test-bottle neck is ruled in percent for a 17.6 c.c. charge; a charge 95 % of that puts up a fat column 95 % as long, read against the same rulings. So every recorded test = 0.95 × true — the tests read **5 % low, one part in twenty** (equivalently, the truth is 1 ÷ 0.95 = 1.0526 × the recorded figure, 5.26 % above it). Vaught's §III/§V value of 16.27 c.c. (ratio 0.9244) is rejected: it is not the mean of the nine readings on the sheet, and his own conclusion says "one part in twenty."

**(b) True average and shortfall.** Recorded average 1898–1922: 3.61 (summary leaf). True = 3.61 ÷ 0.95 = **3.80**. Short by 3.80 − 3.61 = **0.19 of a point** (= 5 % of 3.80). Cross-checks: 1896 on borrowed glass 3.80; the nine weeks of 1911 3.80; 1924 on new glass 3.80; Alder Corners on the same herds ≈ 3.80.

**(c) Pounds not credited.** Milk 1898–1922: 40,000,000 lb (ledgers; 1,600,000 × 25 = 40,000,000).
Credited: 40,000,000 × 0.0361 = **1,444,000 lb**.
Delivered: 40,000,000 × 0.0380 = **1,520,000 lb**.
Not credited: 1,520,000 − 1,444,000 = **76,000 lb** (= 0.0019 × 40,000,000). (Strictly, the nine weeks of 1911 at 3.80 shave a few hundred pounds off this; the sources compute it flat, and so do I.)

**(d) Money and fraction received.** Fat averaged 25¢ over the period (ledger figure; Loomis, Kyle, Roy Brant, Ivy). 76,000 × $0.25 = **$19,000**. Award: $3,800. 3,800 ÷ 19,000 = **1/5 = 20 %**. (The 27¢ of Sill and Kepp is rejected as memory against the ledger; at 27¢ it would be $20,520.)
